scams.name: Fake Parking Ticket QR Code
scams.tldr: Scammers place realistic-looking parking citations with QR codes on out-of-state rental cars near the National Mall and Georgetown — the QR links to a .com payment site that harvests credit card details and charges $75–$150.
scams.description:
You return to your rental car parked on a Georgetown street or near a National Mall lot and find what looks like an official DC parking citation on the windshield. The ticket carries the right logos, color scheme, and formatting, along with a QR code for "fast online payment." Out-of-state plates make you a preferred target because visitors are unfamiliar with how DC citations look.

The QR code leads to a .com website — not a .gov address — that accepts full credit card details and charges $75–$150. Some victims find their card then used for additional unauthorized purchases. The real DC DMV has confirmed it never issues parking tickets; all legitimate citations come from the DC Department of Transportation and are only payable through official .gov portals.

Never scan a QR code from a windshield ticket — go directly to dmv.dc.gov and search your plate number to verify whether a genuine citation exists. Legitimate DC parking tickets show the DC Department of Transportation as the issuing agency, not the DC DMV. Report suspicious citations to the DC DMV at (202) 737-4404.
scams.avoidance: Only pay DC parking tickets through the official DC DMV website at dmv.dc.gov or by mail to the address listed on legitimate tickets. Check the issuing agency: legitimate DC tickets come from the DC Department of Transportation (DDOT) or Metropolitan Police, never from 'DC DMV.' Never scan a QR code on a parking ticket; instead, go directly to the official website and search for your violation by plate number. Take a photo of the ticket and compare it with official DC citation examples available on the DC government website. Report suspicious tickets to the DC DMV at (202) 737-4404 and file a complaint with the Better Business Bureau.
scams.location: Georgetown streets, National Mall parking areas, Dupont Circle metered spots, any street with out-of-state plates

scams.name: Metro Station Change Scam
scams.tldr: In busy Washington DC Metro stations, scammers approach tourists asking to break large bills — then palm the $20 or $50 handed over and claim the tourist gave them a $1, netting $19–$49 in seconds.
scams.description:
You are inside the Smithsonian or Gallery Place Metro station when a man approaches holding two $10 bills: "Can you change this for a $20?" The request sounds ordinary and the busy transit environment creates a sense of routine helpfulness.

You hand over your $20. The scammer palms it instantly and holds up a $1 bill: "You only gave me a dollar." He has switched the bills in a fluid motion. A companion nearby may be creating a secondary distraction at the same moment. Losses range from $19 to $45 per encounter — small enough that most victims do not report it, which is precisely what the operation depends on.

Never make change for a stranger in a Metro station — decline immediately and keep walking. If someone claims to need fare help, point them to the station manager booth. Walk toward the nearest Metro Transit Police officer if anyone becomes persistent.
scams.avoidance: Never make change for strangers in Metro stations or on the street; politely say 'no' and keep walking. If someone needs Metro fare help, direct them to the station manager booth rather than giving cash. Keep large bills in a secure wallet and avoid displaying cash in crowded transit areas. Be especially alert at Smithsonian, Gallery Place, and Union Station Metro stops, which are prime hunting grounds. If you feel pressured, walk toward the station manager booth or a Metro Transit Police officer.
scams.location: Smithsonian Metro station, Gallery Place-Chinatown Metro, Union Station entrance, L'Enfant Plaza Metro concourse

scams.name: Unlicensed Pedicab Price Gouging
scams.tldr: Unlicensed pedicab operators on the National Mall quote no fare upfront, then demand $50–$100 or more after a short ride — operating illegally on National Park Service property where only Tourmobile holds an authorized transportation contract.
scams.description:
You are on the National Mall between the Capitol and Lincoln Memorial — perhaps during cherry blossom season when the crowds make walking difficult — and a pedicab driver pulls alongside offering a ride to the next monument. No price is mentioned before you step in.

At the end of the 10-minute trip the driver demands $80–$120, claiming a "per-minute" rate of $5–$8 that was never disclosed upfront. The NPS grants Tourmobile an exclusive transportation contract on the Mall; most pedicab operators there are unlicensed, meaning they face no regulatory consequences for arbitrary post-ride pricing.

Ask for the per-trip fare in writing before you board any pedicab on the Mall, and photograph the rate card and license number. Licensed operators like Nonpartisan Pedicab post clear hourly rates (around $84–$90 per hour). The DC Circulator bus costs $1 and the Mall is under 2 miles from the Capitol to the Lincoln Memorial — both viable alternatives.
scams.avoidance: Only use pedicab services that display clear per-hour pricing and are licensed by the National Park Service, such as Nonpartisan Pedicab. Always confirm the total fare, whether it is per trip or per hour, and get a verbal agreement before boarding. Take a photo of the rate card and the pedicab's license number before the ride begins. Walk the National Mall instead; the distance from the Capitol to the Lincoln Memorial is about 2 miles and manageable for most visitors. Use the free National Mall shuttle or DC Circulator bus ($1) as cheaper legitimate alternatives.
scams.location: National Mall between the Capitol and Lincoln Memorial, around the Washington Monument, Jefferson Memorial area, Tidal Basin during cherry blossom season

scams.name: Friendship Bracelet and CD Hustle
scams.tldr: Street hustlers near the National Mall and Smithsonian museums tie unsolicited bracelets onto tourists' wrists or press CDs into their hands, then aggressively demand $10–$20 "donations" — sometimes with a pickpocket working the distraction nearby.
scams.description:
You are walking near the Washington Monument or outside a Smithsonian museum when a person approaches with a wide smile. Before you can react, they start tying a colorful bracelet onto your wrist, calling it a "free friendship gift," or they press a CD into your hands claiming they are a local musician who just wants you to hear their work.

Once the item is on your wrist or in your hands, they demand a $10–$20 "donation" and become hostile if you try to return it or walk away. A partner may be standing unusually close during the interaction, reaching toward your pocket or unzipped bag while your attention is fixed on the bracelet or disc.

Keep your hands at your sides or in your pockets near the National Mall, and say "no thank you" without breaking stride. You are not obligated to pay for an item placed on you without consent — if a bracelet is tied on, remove it and set it down. Keep your bag zipped and held in front of your body during any street interaction near the Mall.
scams.avoidance: Keep your hands in your pockets or at your sides and firmly say 'No thank you' without breaking stride. Never allow a stranger to place anything on your body; physically step back if someone reaches for your wrist. If a bracelet is tied on, remove it and place it on the ground; you are not obligated to pay for unsolicited items. Keep your bag zipped and in front of you during any street interaction, especially near the National Mall. If someone becomes aggressive, walk toward the nearest Park Police officer or into a Smithsonian museum entrance.
scams.location: National Mall near the Washington Monument, outside Smithsonian museums, Georgetown M Street, Adams Morgan on weekend nights

scams.name: Three-Card Monte Gambling Hustle
scams.tldr: Teams of four to six people run Three-Card Monte games on DC sidewalks near Union Station and Pennsylvania Avenue — planted shills win visibly to bait tourists, who then lose $50–$300 per round through dealer sleight-of-hand.
scams.description:
You notice a small crowd gathering around a man shuffling three cards on a cardboard box outside Union Station or along Pennsylvania Avenue. Several spectators win easily and wave you over. The energy is festive and the first bets are as low as $10.

Your initial bet wins — the dealer let you win to build confidence. The next bet climbs to $50 or $100. The card you tracked is never where it appears; the dealer uses sleight-of-hand to ensure you lose every significant wager. All the "winning spectators" are paid shills. Lookouts monitor nearby corners for police, and the entire setup can pack up in seconds. Losses typically run $50–$300 per encounter, and victims rarely report the crime.

Never stop to watch Three-Card Monte — even spectators are at risk from pickpockets working the group's perimeter. The MPDC states plainly: "The only time you win is when the suspect lets you." Walk past without engaging and report active operations to Metro Police at (202) 727-9099.
scams.avoidance: Never participate in street gambling games; the game is mathematically rigged through sleight of hand and you cannot win. Walk past without stopping to watch, as even spectators can be targeted by pickpockets working with the group. Understand that the people 'winning' are planted accomplices, not random lucky tourists. Report Three-Card Monte operations to the Metropolitan Police at (202) 727-9099 or 911. Remember that street gambling is illegal in DC and participants can be cited as well as victims.
scams.location: Near Union Station, Gallery Place-Chinatown sidewalks, busy intersections along Pennsylvania Avenue, downtown street corners

scams.name: Fake Tour Guide Solicitation
scams.tldr: Self-appointed "guides" approach tourists outside the White House, Capitol, and Lincoln Memorial, charge $20–$50 per person upfront, then deliver a brief walk with fabricated history — while steering groups into souvenir shops for commissions.
scams.description:
You are outside the White House on Pennsylvania Avenue or near the Capitol steps when a person with a lanyard pitches a private tour: "I know the history of every building on the Mall — better than any app, $30 per person." The approach is confident and the price sounds plausible.

After collecting cash upfront, the guide delivers a 15-minute walk mixing freely available facts with invented anecdotes, then ends the tour early citing a "schedule conflict." Some guides route groups through souvenir shops where they earn commissions, spending more time at the shop than at any monument. Others charge "reservation fees" for the Capitol, Smithsonian museums, and Bureau of Engraving — all of which are entirely free through official channels.

Book tours only through Viator, GetYourGuide, or a company with verifiable reviews — never from someone who approaches you unsolicited near a monument. The National Park Service provides free ranger-led talks and walks at all Mall memorials. Free Capitol, White House, and Bureau of Engraving tours are available through official .gov websites.
scams.avoidance: Book tours only through established companies with verifiable websites, TripAdvisor profiles, and posted reviews. Take advantage of free National Park Service ranger-led walks and talks at all Mall memorials and monuments. Reserve free Capitol, White House, and Bureau of Engraving tours through official.gov websites well in advance. All Smithsonian museums are free; never pay anyone for 'skip the line' access to these institutions. If you want a paid tour, book through platforms like Viator or GetYourGuide where reviews and refund policies are transparent.
scams.location: Outside the White House on Pennsylvania Avenue, near the Capitol steps, around the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool, Arlington Cemetery entrance

scams.name: Distraction Pickpocketing on the Metro
scams.tldr: Two- to three-person teams work Washington DC Metro stations — one bumps or distracts tourists while a partner lifts wallets, phones, or passports — with escalators at Smithsonian and Gallery Place stations being the prime spots.
scams.description:
You are navigating the Metro at Gallery Place-Chinatown or Smithsonian station, phone out and bag open, trying to work out which line to take. The platforms are busy, especially on event days and during cherry blossom season.

A person bumps into you harder than the crowd density justifies, or stops to ask you an oddly complex question while standing very close. A partner behind you or to your side lifts your wallet, phone, or passport while your attention is drawn forward. The "sandwich" technique on escalators — one person in front, one pressing close behind — is also common. Victims typically do not notice the loss until they reach for their wallet at a cafe or museum.

Carry your wallet in a front pocket and keep your bag zipped and held in front of your body at all times on the Metro. Use a money belt for your passport and backup card when touring the city. Report pickpocketing immediately to Metro Transit Police at (202) 962-2121 and cancel stolen cards right away.
scams.avoidance: Carry your wallet in a front pocket and keep your bag zipped and positioned in front of your body at all times on the Metro. Use a money belt or neck wallet for your passport, large cash, and backup credit card when touring the city. Be especially vigilant on escalators at Smithsonian, Metro Center, and Gallery Place stations during peak tourist season. Keep your phone secured and avoid using it while walking through crowded station corridors. Report pickpocketing immediately to Metro Transit Police at (202) 962-2121 and cancel stolen cards right away.
scams.location: Gallery Place-Chinatown station, Metro Center transfer platform, crowded Orange/Blue/Silver line trains, Smithsonian station escalators
